 p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The first atmospheric river of the season arrived in Southern California on Thursday, prompting evacuation warnings on fire-scarred hillsides and concerns about flooded roads and debris flows in foothill communities.
 The storm began inundating roads in San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties overnight and by Thursday morning, a section of Highway 1 in Santa Barbara County was closed, according to the California Department of Transportation.
 “The front is very dynamic and has been a very efficient rain producer with rainfall rates over an inch an hour and half-hour rates near three-quarters of an inch per hour,” the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office posted Thursday morning. “These rates have prompted the issuance of multiple flash flood warnings.”
 Advertisement The storm dumped rain across the Southland all morning Thursday, mucking up the morning commute as drivers maneuvered through water up to the tops of their car tires in the San Fernando Valley. The onslaught prompted firefighters to launch a swift-water rescue attempt in Santa Clarita.
 The California Highway Patrol reported flooding at the 405 and 101 freeway interchange and a debris flow with a large rock on Highway 1 in San Luis Obispo, according to a National Weather Service storm report. Numerous tree branches snapped across Los Angeles due to a powerful thunderstorm.
 When rain falls faster than a half-inch per hour, it has the potential to trigger a mudflow, especially on a hillside that has been burned within the last couple of years.
 Advertisement The concern that the storm could bring rain hard enough to dissolve fire-scarred hillsides into rivers of rock and mud, including in Pacific Palisades, prompted a flash flood warning for southwest L.A. County that expired at noon. It was replaced with a flash flood advisory until 6 p.m..
 The storm comes amid a historically strong El Niño that has already warmed ocean waters and elevated sea levels. The climate pattern tilts the odds toward a wetter-than-normal winter in Southern California.
 California 
 For Subscribers What the El Niño worst-case scenario would look like in California 
 The extensive coastal flooding that swamped Los Angeles and Orange counties recently was influenced by an El Niño-powered global-scale phenomenon known as a Kelvin wave, scientists confirmed.
 Nov. 2, 2026 Overnight, the storm knocked over trees in San Luis Obispo and Summerland, flooded a section of Highway 101, trapping a vehicle, and triggered multiple rock slides, according to the weather service.
 Before the storm moved into Los Angeles County early Thursday, portions of Ventura County were thoroughly soaked, said Mike Wofford, a meteorologist for the National Weather Service in Oxnard.
 At around 5 a.m., he said, rain fell in foothill and mountain communities, including Ojai and Fillmore, at a rate of more than an inch an hour, and Oxnard got more than seven-tenths of an inch per hour. 
 The morning drenching included “the heaviest rain band” within the system, he said, adding that scattered rainfall and light showers were on tap for the afternoon and evening. 
 Advertisement “This is really the big show coming through now,” he said at about 7:45 a.m. Thursday, as the storm made its way through Los Angeles County. 
 Ahead of the storm, residents in the communities most vulnerable to a debris flow — including those living near the burn scars of the Eaton fire in Altadena, the Palisades fire near Pacific Palisades, Malibu and Topanga, the Sunset fire in the Hollywood Hills, the Kenneth fire in Calabasas, the Hurst fire near Sylmar and the Canyon fire near Hasley Canyon, Castaic and Val Verde — were contacted and told to prepare to leave, according to the county Office of Emergency Services. 
 The warning remains in place through 8 a.m. Friday.
 All residents are encouraged to stay away from flood control channels, catch basins, canyons and natural waterways that are vulnerable to flooding, the Office of Emergency Services said.
 Early Thursday, a woman stranded on an island in the surging Tujunga Wash was rescued by a Los Angeles Fire Department air crew, with a rescuer suspended by rope to hoist her up and take her to dry land, said Lyndsey Lantz, a department spokeswoman. The woman was taken to a hospital, but her condition was unknown, Lantz said.
 LAFD crews also saved a man and his dog trapped in their car in about 1 1/2 feet of standing water, she said.
 Although the rain had started to slow by mid-morning, Lantz said, there was “heavy, heavy water in the flood channels” that posed a major risk for homeless people camping near waterways. 
 Advertisement Earlier in the week, California activated its State Operations Center to coordinate an administration-wide response to the potential heavy rain and flooding, according to the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services, which also said the state put more resources closer to at-risk communities ahead of the storm. The office approves the prepositioning of local government fire department personnel and equipment, including engines and swift water rescue teams.
 Northern California caught the first of the bad weather, pelted by heavy rain that left cars stalled in floodwaters Wednesday.
 Dramatic footage of vehicles submerged in San Francisco — from self-driving Waymos to U.S. Postal Service mail delivery trucks — circulated on social media and in local news reports. An underground Muni Metro station was closed for more than two hours due to flooding.
 Wofford said the weekend “is looking great” in Southern California, with cooler mornings and clear skies.
